title: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat warns against ‘regime change’ bid, cites France, Bangladesh and Nepal - Firstpost
description: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat warns against ‘regime change’ bid, cites France, Bangladesh and Nepal  Firstpost
publisher.title: Firstpost
full_article:
RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Tuesday warned against attempts to bring about “regime change” in India, citing unrest in countries such as France, Bangladesh and Nepal.

His remarks come amid a political row over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, with some demonstrators calling for a change of government.

Addressing the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s annual Vijayadashami gathering, Bhagwat said that similar attempts were being made in India but asserted that the country would not follow the same path.

“Regime change will not happen in India. Such attempts continue in India as well,” he said, adding that the country had moved forward through determination and the collective strength of its people.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Bhagwat also said protests should focus on resolving problems rather than creating hostility.

He called for dialogue and mutual understanding, arguing that movements driven by electoral gains or the pursuit of popularity could not offer lasting solutions.

Bhagwat warns of forces seeking to create unrest

The RSS chief alleged that various forces were trying to fuel discontent, encourage a sense of victimhood and create confusion in society. He urged people to remain alert against attempts to divide the country.

“These demonic forces know this, and that is why India is their target,” Bhagwat said, alleging that such forces wanted to weaken India, Hindus and the RSS.

More from India

He also accused people with vested interests and ambitious political leaders of supporting these efforts.

Bhagwat stressed the need to preserve India's unity while respecting its diversity. He said people should move beyond individual egos and misconceptions about different forms of worship, and avoid treating diversity as a source of division.

He identified devotion to Bharat, pride in the country's ancestors and commitment to Bharatiya culture as common bonds that could bring people together. He also called for continued efforts to help India achieve the status of Vishwaguru.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised Bhagwat's Vijayadashami address, describing it as “highly inspiring”.

Advertisement

Advertisement

In a post on X, PM Modi highlighted the RSS chief's remarks on national progress, social unity, self-reliance and service. He also referred to Panch Parivartan, the RSS's emphasis on five areas of social change.

Prashant Bhushan's remarks trigger political row

Bhagwat's comments come after senior advocate Prashant Bhushan described the ongoing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as a “fight for regime change” on October 15.

Speaking at a press conference with Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and other activists, Bhushan defended the demand, saying citizens had the democratic right to seek a change of government.

“Yes, we all want regime change. What is wrong with that?” he said, arguing that the agitation was about protecting electoral democracy.

The remarks prompted a strong response from the BJP. The party accused the protesters and their political supporters of attempting to remove the Narendra Modi government without an electoral mandate.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh also alleged that some groups were seeking regime change along the lines of developments in Bangladesh and attempting to destabilise democratic institutions.

KATHMANDU — Bhadai Tharu says he still remembers the day a tiger attacked him. It was around 1 p.m. on Jan. 6, 2004. The encounter left him blind in his left eye.

More than two decades later, the 59-year-old doesn’t speak ill of the animal that attacked him.

“When incidents, like the one I was involved in, happen, people get angry,” says Tharu, who is now chair of the Gauri Community Forest on the fringes of Bardiya National Park, a global hotspot for the endangered big cats.

“Tigers have their role in the ecosystem, and both people and tigers should coexist,” Tharu says.

His perspective comes as Nepal’s tiger population reaches a record 429 individuals, with Bardiya alone hosting 112. To avoid human-tiger encounters such as the one Tharu experienced, researchers turned to a survival skill long practiced by local people: listening to the forest. And for a while, at least, it seemed to have worked.

The pilot project, documented in a recently published study, tested an artificial intelligence-powered system that “listens” to alarm calls from chital deer ( Axis axis ) and maps areas where tigers ( Panthera tigris ) or leopards ( Panthera pardus ) may be present and that humans should avoid.

A chital deer in Bardiya National Park. The pilot project tested an AI-powered system that “listens” to alarm calls from chital deer. Image by Sunuwargr via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

A forest that speaks

Long before researchers arrived with sensors and machine-learning models, Indigenous communities in Bardiya had already been listening to the forest.

“Footprints, scat, and alarm calls from deer, langurs, red monkeys all tell us that a tiger may be nearby,” Tharu says.

In his experience, the warning often begins with rhesus macaques ( Macaca mulatta ), known locally as red monkeys. “They become restless first, and then the deer respond,” Tharu says.

According to study co-author Ramjan Chaudhary, a field biologist with the Bardia Nature Conservation Club, a local community organization, interpreting alarm calls has long been common among nature guides, forest guards, and residents living near wildlife habitat.

Co-author Casey Anderson, a U.S.-based wildlife filmmaker and conservationist who led the deployment of the project, says the team sought to automate knowledge that communities already make use of.

“We weren’t teaching the forest or the people who live there something new,” he says. “In many ways, we were teaching a computer to recognize something those people already understood.”

The researchers deployed acoustic monitoring devices throughout the Dalla Community Forest neighboring Bardiya National Park, and carried out their predator-response experiments there and in the Khata Community forest, including parts of the Khata International Biological Corridor linking Nepal and India.

A faux tiger skin used as a predator model for chital deer. Image by Kershenbaum et al. / Zoological Society of London & Wiley (CC BY-NC-ND).

Turning alarm calls into data

Rather than tracking tigers directly, the researchers focused on how prey species respond to them.

“Sometimes the best way to find a predator isn’t to look for the predator itself. It’s to listen to everything around it,” Anderson says.

Using a tiger model, the team tested whether prey species produced alarm calls when confronted with a predator. Chital deer, rhesus macaques, and Tarai gray langurs ( Semnopithecus hector ) consistently responded with alarm calls during encounters with the model, suggesting that those vocalizations could act as indicators of predator risk. Researchers also noted that prey don’t always vocalize when predators are present, meaning alarm calls may not capture every encounter.

The team then trained a lightweight AI model to recognize chital deer alarm calls on solar-powered monitoring devices, which cost about $60 each.

When an alarm call was detected, the system transmitted information through a wireless network and generated a map highlighting areas where tigers or leopards might be present. The researchers deployed 10 of the monitoring units throughout Dalla Community Forest for three months.

“The ultimate objective was never simply to locate tigers. It was to reduce dangerous encounters between people and predators,” Anderson says.

An acoustic recording device deployed in the Dalla community forest. Right: the inside of the device showing the various components. Image by Kershenbaum et al. / Zoological Society of London & Wiley (CC BY-NC-ND).

Shared landscapes

These forests are used by both wildlife and people.

Residents collect firewood, harvest fiddlehead ferns known locally as niuro , and other forest products while grazing livestock in areas also used by tigers, leopards, elephants ( Elephas maximus ), and rhinos ( Rhinoceros unicornis ).

“People use the forest for grass and fodder,” Tharu says. “They keep pigs and goats, and their livelihoods depend on the forest.”

Human-tiger conflict remains a persistent challenge. A recent study found that tigers attacked 245 people in Nepal between 2010 and 2024, killing 141 of them, while another documented 18 deaths and 10 injuries around Bardiya National Park between 2019 and 2023.

Communities hail promising technology

For local forest users, the technology made immediate sense as it reflected knowledge they were already using. Thenghchu Tharu, a 60-year-old forest guard at the Dalla Community Forest who helped monitor the pilot project, says he’s relied for years on alarm calls from chital deer to gauge predator presence.

“When chital repeatedly call out, we know there may be a tiger or leopard nearby,” he says.

During the pilot project, he compared the system’s alerts with signs observed on the ground: “It matched exactly.”

When alerts suggested tiger presence in a particular area, residents could be warned to stay away temporarily.

A village in the buffer zone next to Chitwan National Park. Image by Jonas Gratzer for Mongabay.

“We would tell people there is a tiger there and not to go because it could be dangerous,” Thenghchu Tharu says.

He adds he believes the system could reduce risky encounters for people entering the forest to collect fodder, gather firewood, or graze their livestock.

“If people are informed beforehand, they do not need to enter that area,” he says.

Study co-author Chaudhary says communities responded positively to the project and were “enthusiastic about seeing this new technology in action.”

Bhadai Tharu, the tiger-attack survivor, shares that view. “We were happy to see it. It was very good.”

He says he believes the technology could save lives. “It can save people from attacks. When people are informed beforehand, incidents can be reduced.”

Why the pilot ended

Yet despite the positive feedback from communities and encouraging results, the system was never expanded in Nepal.

“We expected it would still be implemented, but it never happened,” Bhadai Tharu says.

Several community members interviewed for this story expressed disappointment that the project ended after the trial phase. Anderson says the problem was not a rejection of the technology itself.

“I wouldn’t characterize it as Nepal deciding not to pursue the technology or as a failure of the concept,” he says.

Instead, he says, the project struggled to secure the staffing, funding, and local institutional support needed to move beyond a proof of concept.

“As the initial project’s resources began to run out, we weren’t able to establish the local staffing and university involvement necessary to keep it operating,” Anderson says.

The equipment was later moved to India, where researchers had an opportunity to continue testing and refining the concept.

“There was an opportunity to continue exploring and developing the concept in India, so moving the equipment allowed the work to continue rather than simply ending when that particular phase in Nepal concluded,” Anderson says.

Officials have taken a more cautious view. Sabnam Pathak, information officer at Nepal’s Department of Forests and Soil Conservation, says new conservation technologies need long-term evaluation before wider adoption, adding they should only be deployed “after a thorough study.”

The study itself acknowledged several limitations, including false detections, equipment failures, and overheating problems. Alarm calls can indicate predator risk, but can’t reliably distinguish whether a tiger or a leopard triggered them. In some cases, deer fled without vocalizing, meaning predator presence could go undetected.

Shyam Kumar Thapa, program manager at the Nepal office of the Zoological Society of London (ZSL), says the challenge goes beyond protected areas.

“The most serious concern is the escalation of these interactions into human fatalities and retaliatory killing of tigers,” he says.

He adds the technology could help shift the management of human-wildlife conflict from a reactive approach to a more proactive one by helping authorities and communities anticipate risk before dangerous encounters occur.

Anderson says he believes technology can help amplify those efforts.

“It isn’t artificial intelligence replacing human knowledge,” he says. “It’s artificial intelligence helping us listen more effectively to the natural intelligence that has always been there.”

title: Why did Nepal bar screening Sara Ali Khan, Ayushmann Khurrana’s 'Udta Teer'? - The Week
description: Why did Nepal bar screening Sara Ali Khan, Ayushmann Khurrana’s 'Udta Teer'?  The Week
publisher.title: The Week
full_article:
Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan’s upcoming spy comedy film Udta Teer has hit a roadblock in Nepal, ahead of its worldwide theatrical release on Friday.

The film was denied permission for public screening following a review by Nepal’s Central Film Censor Board. The regulatory authority reportedly found the film to violate a provision of the country’s cinema law.

Nepal’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology sent a letter to the film’s local distributor, National Cine Group Nepal, explaining the ministry’s decision to stop the screening. The censor board’s assessment was final, with the ministry refusing to grant permission for the film’s public screening.

According to media reports, the Ministry of Audio-visual and Broadcasting stated that the film’s content is prohibited under Section 8(3) of the Film (Production, Exhibition and Distribution) Act, 1963. The Section states that the film censor board cannot approve a film that might potentially disturb Nepal’s security, peace and order, relations with friendly countries or harmony among different classes or ethnic groups.

Nepali film writer and critic Samipyaraj Timilsina, who talked to Global Newsflix, said the Central Film Censor Board reportedly denied the film permission because its sensitive storyline explored tensions between India and Pakistan.

Nepal maintains a neutral stance during conflicts between India and Pakistan.

The film, directed by Aakash Kaushik and produced by Dharma Productions, follows a Pakistani spy who loses his memory in India and begins believing that he is an Indian counterterrorism officer and develops a sense of patriotism.

The Aamir Khan-produced Bantwara 1947, which follows a Muslim family displaced during the partition, was also temporarily put on hold by Nepal’s Central Film Screening Committee. Though the regulatory authorities never explicitly objected to the film’s storyline, the movie's geopolitical themes are allegedly sensitive.

While the film will face public screening restrictions in Nepal, it is set to release in India on October 23.

title: Far from home, Dashain carries a different kind of ache - The Kathmandu Post
description: Far from home, Dashain carries a different kind of ache  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Last year, when cherry blossoms were in season in Japan, I called my father in Nepal. I had not been home for more than two years, and with Dashain approaching, I was wondering whether I could afford to return.

“Should I come home for Dashain this year, Baba?” I asked. “Do you need to ask permission to come home? Of course, come.”

“I came abroad to repay the loan we took to build our house. It is still unpaid. If I come home, the debt will only grow. That is why I am asking.”

“Your elder brother is there to look after all that. And I am here, above your brother.” His words were full of reassurance. I had nothing more to say.

“Who knows who will be alive next year and who won't? You'll get to see everyone. Come home, yes, come.”

He hung up.

After 28 months in Japan, I returned to Nepal for Dashain in 2023. I celebrated the festival with my family and spent a month at home before returning to Japan.

In July 2024, my father died. That October, there would be no Dashain with him.

I often find myself returning to that telephone conversation. Did he somehow know he would not live to see another Dashain? Was that why he had insisted I come home while I still could? When he said, “Who knows who will be alive next year and who won't?”, he may have been speaking about the uncertainty of life in general. But now, those words sound like a farewell he did not know he was giving.

***

It was October 12, 2024. Dashain was underway in Nepal, and we were celebrating it too, thousands of miles away, on an open patch of ground beside the Motoyasu river in Hiroshima, Japan.

The river carries a history of unimaginable suffering. At 8.15am on August 6, 1945, the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. The explosion shook the earth and unleashed intense heat, burning people where they stood. In the chaos that followed, many desperately sought water. Some plunged into the Motoyasu and other nearby rivers, hoping to escape the flames. Many died there.

That day, however, we had gathered beside the river for a different reason. We had come to celebrate Dashain, Nepal’s biggest Hindu festival, far from the country, families and familiar rituals that gave it meaning.

We were in our second year at a Japanese language school. When we first arrived, it took us time to get to know one another. The previous year, in 2023, we had celebrated Dashain at the school, where a Japanese teacher had put tika on our foreheads. Even that small gesture had made a little flower of happiness bloom in a corner of my heart.

This year felt different. We had grown closer, perhaps because we had shared more of one another's struggles. From the following March, in 2025, we would go our separate ways to attend senmon gakkō, or professional training colleges, in different places. After two years of Japanese language classes, moving on to vocational education was the expected next step.

Our time together was drawing to a close, and the festival felt like an occasion to hold on to one another a little longer.

Some friends arrived looking as if they had not slept all night. Others turned up with half-closed eyes, having managed only a few hours of rest. Some came straight from work. Others arrived with their bags packed, saying they would head to work directly from the gathering later that evening.

No one's feet were rested. Even when tired, we had to keep moving. Even when we stumbled, we had to get back up and run towards the distant destinations we had set for ourselves.

And no one's heart was entirely at ease. We missed home, the festivals and the people we had left behind. Everyone carried a private burden. A month's wages barely covered monthly expenses for some of us, while debts back in our villages continued to weigh on our minds. Under such circumstances, even thinking about spending money on a festival could feel like a luxury.

Yet we had gathered here, determined to celebrate.

***

A year earlier, around Dashain in 2023, young Nepalis from different districts had come together in Japan, most of us strangers to one another. In the space of a year, those unfamiliar faces had become familiar, almost like family.

Our friends Sarina, Sabina and Shila brought meat, roti and vegetables they had cooked in their rooms. Before they arrived, the boys' group had already settled in with cans of beer. Some friends, carried away by the drink and the excitement, had begun dancing with their arms around one another.

“Dashain is here!” someone sang, and the others joined in.

For a while, the riverbank became a little piece of Nepal.

We mixed red tika and prepared to bless one another. By age, I turned out to be the oldest among the group. One by one, my friends came forward to receive tika from my hand.

At home, Dashain is marked by rituals that have been passed down through generations. Elders put tika and jamara on the foreheads of younger family members and bless them for health, happiness and prosperity. Families reunite, relatives visit one another, and homes fill with the sounds of conversation, laughter and celebration.

Here, we had none of the usual surroundings. There was no family courtyard, no familiar home, no elder waiting to put tika on our foreheads. We had only one another.

But as each friend bowed his or her head before me, I felt the significance of what we were doing. We were not simply recreating a festival from home. We were trying to preserve a sense of belonging in a place where most things remained unfamiliar.

The tika was a small gesture, but it connected us to our families, our villages and the lives we had left behind.

***

When I lived in Nepal, I had relatives, a house and a place to call home, but little money. In Japan, I had some money, but no home in the same sense and no relatives close at hand.

Life, I have come to realise, is a constant negotiation between what we have and what we lack. The balance never quite settles.

Back in my village, the smell of ripening paddy in the fields was one of the first signs that Dashain was approaching. The crowds heading to the market, buying clothes and provisions for the festival, made the season feel closer. The village would begin to take on a different mood. There was a sense of anticipation in the air.

Abroad, the same season brought a different kind of awareness. A Dashain song playing in the background could suddenly make me miss home so much that it hurt. I thought of friends and relatives, of familiar paths and the ordinary routines I had once taken for granted. Photographs and videos of people playing on traditional Dashain swings, shared repeatedly on social media, stirred up memories I did not know I was carrying so deeply.

When I was in Nepal, I never imagined that living abroad would make me miss so many things. Back then, I thought how wonderful it would be to get the chance to go overseas. I believed that reaching a foreign country would open the door to a better life.

Now, living in Japan, I often find myself thinking how wonderful it would be to go home.

Perhaps that is the nature of longing. When we are in one place, we dream of another. When we have a home but little money, we dream of earning abroad. Once abroad, with some money in our pockets, we long for the home and people we left behind.

We spend our lives reaching for what is missing, often discovering its true value only after it is gone.

***

As I stood beside the Motoyasu river with my friends, celebrating Dashain in October 2024, far from Nepal, I thought again of my father.

In 2023, I had returned home because he had urged me to. I had worried about the debt, the expense of travelling and the money I would lose by taking time off work. He had looked beyond all of that. He wanted me home while we still had the chance to be together.

I did not know then that it would be my last Dashain with him.

When I see photographs of Dashain celebrations in Nepal, I think of my father and the family I left behind. We often postpone going home because of debts, work and the need to save money, believing there will always be another Dashain. But life does not always give us another chance.

Here, beside the Motoyasu River, we celebrate with friends who have become a kind of family. We share food, laughter and tika, yet home remains somewhere far away, in the people and places we miss.

When we lived in Nepal, we dreamed of going abroad. Now, in Japan, we dream of going home. Perhaps that is the strange hunger of life: we long for what we do not have, only to realise its worth when it is out of reach.

full_article:
Swarnim Wagle, Nepal's finance minister, economist and vice-chairperson of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), will speak at the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi on October 23.

He will speak at 11:15 am on Day 2 of the summit in a session titled “Proximity to Prosperity: The India-Nepal Opportunity”. The summit will be held on October 22 and 23.

Who is Dr Swarnim Wagle?

Wagle was born in 1974 in Bungkot, Gorkha, Nepal. He studied economics at the London School of Economics, where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree. He later completed a master's degree in international development at Harvard University. He also earned a PhD in economics from the Australian National University.

Wagle was elected Member of Parliament (MP) from Tanahun-1 constituency for a second consecutive term in March 2026. He was also elected unopposed as vice-chairperson of the Rastriya Swatantra Party at its first general convention. He now serves as Nepal's Finance Minister.

Before joining politics, Wagle worked with international organisations for over 25 years. He worked as a senior economist at the World Bank in Washington, DC. He also served as chief economic adviser at the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in New York. He has worked on development projects and policy issues in more than 20 countries.

Wagle joined Nepal's National Planning Commission in 2014. He served as a member and later became its vice-chairperson. He worked with the commission for three years between 2014 and 2018.

After a major earthquake hit Nepal in 2015, Wagle co-led a team that assessed the damage and the money needed to rebuild the country. He also led Nepal's team at the Third UN Conference on Financing for Development.

From 2002 to 2007, he co-led a UNDP programme focused on trade and investment in the Asia-Pacific region. The programme also worked on issues linked to World Trade Organization negotiations. He took up assignments with the Asian Development Bank in Manila and the International Trade Center in Geneva.

Wagle has written several reports and research papers on the economy, trade, investment and public policy. He co-authored the UNDP's 2013 Human Development Report, titled The Rise of the South. He also co-edited The Great Upheaval, published by Cambridge University Press in 2022. He was the South Asia editor of Harvard Asia Quarterly from around 1999 to 2000.

From 2019 to 2026, Wagle led the Institute for Integrated Development Studies (IIDS), a policy research organisation based in Kathmandu. It was established in 1979. He is now its chairman emeritus. He has also served as a senator at Kathmandu University and has advised several non-profit organisations. He has been associated with the World Bank's South Asia Champions Group and the South Asia Regional Champions.

NDTV World Summit 2026

The NDTV World Summit 2026 will be held in New Delhi on October 22 and 23. The summit will bring together political leaders, economists, policymakers and other global voices to discuss important issues facing India and the world.

The theme of the summit is “A World Between Orders”. The discussions will focus on changes in the global order, international relations, the world economy and the challenges facing countries.

title: 'They went to jail smiling': Dipke rebuts Nepal, Bangladesh parallels - Rediff
description: 'They went to jail smiling': Dipke rebuts Nepal, Bangladesh parallels  Rediff
publisher.title: Rediff
full_article:
Rejecting claims that local demonstrations mirror international turmoil, Dipke defended jailed activists Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, saying their calm compliance was proof of a purely Gandhian Satyagraha.

IMAGE: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke leaves after being granted bail, following his appearance before the special executive magistrate court at Mandir Marg police station, in New Delhi, October 17, 2026. Photograph: Amit/ANI Photo

Amid escalating debate comparing youth protests in India to political unrest and regime changes in Nepal and Bangladesh, Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) activist Abhijeet Dipke on Tuesday issued a video statement on X.

Key Points Dipke urged observers to look at the adherence to non-violence displayed by Indian dissidents.

Refusing to equate domestic civil dissent with violent overthrows, Dipke argued that the conduct of the imprisoned activists distinguishes Indian civil resistance from foreign movements.

Dipke maintained that preventive detentions and prison terms would fail to break the morale of the movement or push it toward violence.

Rejecting claims that local demonstrations mirror international turmoil, Dipke defended jailed activists Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, saying their calm compliance was proof of a purely Gandhian Satyagraha.

Addressing critics and commentators who cite global political volatility, ranging from violent youth riots in France to regime-change movements in Bangladesh and Nepal, Dipke urged observers to look at the adherence to non-violence displayed by Indian dissidents.

"To those constantly pointing fingers saying, 'Look at what is happening in France...' have some shame and look at what is happening right here in India. In India, Sourav Das and Ashutosh went to jail with smiles on their faces. They didn't do anything like what is happening elsewhere. Even when they knew they were being unlawfully imprisoned, they chose peace and compassion, entering prison with smiles rather than anger or hatred in their hearts," Dipke said.

Refusing to equate domestic civil dissent with violent overthrows, Dipke argued that the conduct of the imprisoned activists distinguishes Indian civil resistance from foreign movements.

"People talk about Nepal or Bangladesh, but look at our comrades: they went to jail smiling, without being provoked. They continue to embody Gandhian values—smiling on their way to jail, smiling inside the courtroom. You cannot instil hatred in them; hatred resides in you. And everyone can clearly see the state to which your hatred has brought this country," he added.

Dipke framed the activists' imprisonment not as a tool for chaotic overthrow, but as a moral awakening rooted in India’s historic independence struggle.

"Without wanting to draw direct comparisons, it reflects what Mahatma Gandhi did; when he was sent to jail, he went quietly because it was his Satyagraha. Ashutosh and Sourav are carrying out that exact same Satyagraha. By enduring that pain inside prison, they are awakening the conscience of this country. I cannot wait for them to be released," he stated.

Addressing state authorities and political opponents who view public gatherings as a threat to order, Dipke maintained that preventive detentions and prison terms would fail to break the morale of the movement or push it toward violence.

"If anyone thinks locking Sourav and Ashutosh up will intimidate or break them, that is never going to happen. I assure you, when they walk out, they will emerge with the same smiles, chanting 'Inquilab Zindabad' (Long Live the Revolution), continuing on Mahatma Gandhi's path of peace and non-violence—values we deeply believe in," Dipke added.

The judicial custody of Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka was extended by two days after their initial five-day judicial custody ended on Monday.

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were taken back to judicial custody from Mandir Marg Police Station in Delhi after their surety was rejected over a reported mismatch in documents, their lawyers said. Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) Court situated at Police Station Mandir Marg extended the custody till October 21.

Meanwhile, a Fox News Digital investigation published on October 9 identified 50 organisations associated with France's student protest movement and its wider network of supporters, alleging that communist, socialist and far-left groups are using demonstrations over school conditions to advance broader political and ideological agendas.

The Congress has strongly dismissed attempts to link ongoing opposition protests against the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise to the violent civil unrest sweeping France and other European nations, asserting that the opposition’s movement is strictly peaceful, constitutional, and centred on free and fair elections.

The sharp pushback from the Congress came after the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) alleged a coordinated conspiracy by "anti-India gangs" to orchestrate "regime change" in India similar to the recent turmoil in Bangladesh and France.

title: Udta Teer Denied Release Clearance In Nepal Ahead Of Theatrical Debut - News Mobile
description: Udta Teer Denied Release Clearance In Nepal Ahead Of Theatrical Debut  News Mobile
publisher.title: News Mobile
full_article:
New Delhi: Actors Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan’s upcoming film Udta Teer has been denied permission for public screening in Nepal ahead of its scheduled theatrical release. The decision was taken after Nepal’s Central Film Censor Board found that the film’s content fell under restrictions specified in the country’s cinema law.

An official letter issued by Nepal’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology to film distributor National Cine Group Nepal states that the film cannot be publicly screened under Section 8(3) of the National Cinema (Production, Exhibition and Distribution) Act, 2026.

According to the letter, the film was examined by the Central Film Censor Board based on the material submitted for review. The board found that its content fell under a category restricted by the law and, therefore, decided not to grant permission for public exhibition.

Udta Teer was scheduled to release in cinemas on Friday. The film is directed by Aakash Kaushik and is slated to release in India on October 23.

Why Has Udta Teer Been Denied Permission In Nepal?

According to reports, Udta Teer deals with tensions between India and Pakistan. The film’s subject is believed to have prompted the censor board’s decision, although the ministry’s letter does not specify the exact scenes or content that led to the restriction.

Nepal’s cinema laws include provisions that can restrict films if their content is considered to affect the national interests or communities of a country. Consequently, Udta Teer has not been granted permission for public screening in Nepal.

The decision comes ahead of the film’s planned theatrical release, leaving its Nepal release uncertain.

Udta Teer stars Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan in the lead roles. Directed by Aakash Kaushik, the film is scheduled for release in Indian cinemas on October 23.
